big_idea: 3D shapes are SOLID. Sphere, cube, cylinder, cone, pyramid. They have faces, edges, vertices.
learning_intention: We are learning to identify and describe 3D shapes.
student_learning_goal: I can identify and describe 3D shapes.
success_criteria: I can describe a 3D shape (faces, edges, points).
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Sammy and Mira — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 2 3D tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Sammy holds a SPHERE — like a real ball. What other 3D shapes can we find?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Sammy + Mira puppets. 'Yesterday we hunted FLAT 2D shapes. Today we hunt SOLID 3D shapes.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write 3D on chart. '3D shapes are SOLID — like real objects. They have faces (flat sides), edges (where faces meet), and vertices (corner points).'

Show each 3D shape:
'SPHERE — like a ball. Round all over. No flat faces.'
'CUBE — like a dice. 6 equal flat faces. 8 corners.'
'CYLINDER — like a can. 2 round faces, 1 curved face.'
'CONE — like an ice cream cone. 1 round face, 1 point.'
'PYRAMID — like a tent. Triangle faces meeting at a point.'

Compare to 2D. 'A circle is FLAT. A sphere is SOLID. A square is FLAT. A cube is SOLID.'

Real-life examples: 'Cube = dice, Tim Hortons box. Cylinder = soup can, Tim Hortons coffee cup. Cone = traffic cone. Sphere = hockey puck (well, that's a cylinder!). Pyramid = museum.'

Sammy's RULE: 'NAME IT — count SIDES — count CORNERS!' For 3D: count FACES instead of sides; count VERTICES instead of corners.

Class refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'NAME IT — count SIDES — count CORNERS! That's how Sammy hunts!'

'Today we identify 3D shapes around us.'
student_actions: Listen to Sammy and Mira name 3D shapes.

steps.instruction: Whole group: identify 5 3D shapes by handling.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Touch. Count faces. Name the shape.'

steps.instruction: Three stations. Station A: Match 3D models to names. Station B: 2D vs 3D sort. Station C: Find 3D shapes in classroom.
Stretch challenge at Station C: count faces of each 3D shape.
Discuss faces, edges, vertices. 'Cube: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Show shape anchor chart with 3D properties.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the 3D tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. 3 shapes only (sphere, cube, cylinder).
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: count faces AND describe the difference between a 3D shape and its 2D 'shadow' (e.g., a cube casts a square shadow).
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Sentence frame: 'A ___ has ___ faces and ___ corners.' Pre-teach with hand gestures (sphere = round hands; cube = box; cylinder = tall round can; cone = ice cream pointer; pyramid = tent peak).
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-PURCHASE PATH: skip the printed shape models and the printed sort/match cards entirely. Children HUNT the classroom for real 3D shapes — point at the dice, the soup can, the ball, the cone, the box-shaped tissue box; they BODY-MIME each shape (round-arm = sphere; box-arms = cube; tall-can = cylinder; cone hands meeting overhead = pyramid). Whole lesson runs on bodies + the existing classroom — no purchased models, no printed cards.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: names 5 3D shapes; describes properties; distinguishes 2D from 3D.

discussion_prompts: How is a cube different from a square?
What 3D shapes did you find in the classroom?
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. Then each child names ONE 3D shape and ONE property: 'My ___ has ___ faces and ___ corners.' Sticky-note one 3D shape and post on the Shape Safari poster.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child confuses 2D and 3D names — repairing the dimension confusion at K (van Hiele, 1986; Clements & Sarama, 2009; Lehrer et al., 1998)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A9.2 3D shape identification, the most-documented K trap is the dimension confusion: child calls a sphere a 'circle' or a cube a 'square'. They have not yet differentiated 2D (flat) from 3D (solid) as separate mathematical categories.

Van Hiele's (1986) Level-0 (Visualization) describes this exactly: K children identify shapes by overall visual appearance, and a 3D ball viewed head-on looks like a 2D circle. The dimensional category — 'is this FLAT like paper or SOLID like a real object?' — has not yet been added to their identification routine. The repair is to add the 'flat or solid?' check as the FIRST step of every shape ID.

Clements & Sarama (2009) place 2D-3D differentiation as a key K transition in the geometric thinking trajectory: children who exit K still calling spheres 'circles' arrive in Grade 1 unable to engage with 3D measurement (volume) or 3D building. The fix at K is sensorimotor — children must HOLD spheres, ROLL cylinders, STACK cubes; the embodied difference between flat-on-paper and solid-in-hand is what dislodges the visualization-only category.

Lehrer et al. (1998) on 'building elaborated knowledge of geometric figures' show that K children who use property-based language (faces, edges, vertices) develop more flexible geometric thinking by Grade 2 than children who only use prototype names. The vocabulary introduced here — 'face' for a flat surface of a 3D shape, 'edge' where two faces meet, 'vertex' for a corner point — is foundational, not merely descriptive.

Why this matters: a K child who exits with 2D-3D fused will bottleneck Grade 1-2 measurement, building, and shape-composition tasks. The repair must happen at K with embodied 3D handling.

The walkthrough covers when child calls a sphere a circle.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B. Child holds a sphere model. Says 'circle'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Hmm — a circle is FLAT, like paper. This ball is SOLID. Squeeze it. Roll it. It's a SPHERE.'

Walk through. 'Sphere is the SOLID version of a circle. Cube is the SOLID version of a square. Cylinder is solid like a can — has 2 circles and a curved side.'

The child re-names. Generalise. 'Sammy says — flat shapes are 2D. Solid shapes are 3D. Even if they look similar from one side.'

If still confused: provide a 2D-3D pair card. 'Circle (2D) | Sphere (3D)'. Show both side by side.

Long-term recovery: every shape ID checks 'flat or solid?' first.
expected_student_responses: (Stretched) Lists faces and edges of each 3D shape.
common_misconceptions: Square box = square. (Repair: solid box = cube.)
All shapes are the same. (Repair: flat vs solid.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child uses 2D names for 3D shapes (van Hiele Level-0 visualization, no dimensional check): use 2D-3D pair cards (circle | sphere; square | cube; triangle | pyramid). Show both side-by-side; have child point at FLAT and SOLID; ask 'flat or solid?' before naming. Repeat for the next 3 shapes until 'flat or solid?' becomes the first step.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child can name 3D shape but cannot count faces (no Lehrer et al. 1998 property-based language yet): hand them a cube; child points at and counts each FACE one by one (top, bottom, 4 sides = 6); record the count on the anchor chart. Repeat with cylinder (2 round + 1 curved = 3 faces) and pyramid (4 triangles + 1 square base = 5).

DIAGNOSTIC C — child confuses cylinder with cone or sphere with cube under handling (poor sensorimotor differentiation, Clements & Sarama 2009): blindfold trial — child closes eyes, teacher places one of 5 3D shapes in their hands; child names by feel only. Do this for 3 shapes per child; the embodied differentiation is what locks the 3D category.

parts_outline.task: Find and draw 3 3D shapes from your classroom.
